The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is [[thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-radon-nikodym]] and uniqueness is [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]], applied to [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The quotient is [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. The [[def-axiom-of-choice]] assumption is inherited from RN existence.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **p-value
statistic** is a statistic $p:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, where $[0,1]$ carries the
trace of the Borel sigma-algebra, meaning
$\{B\cap[0,1]:B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

For a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, the statistic is a
**valid p-value for $\Theta_0$** if it is superuniform under every null law:
$$P_\theta(\{x:p(x)\le u\})\le u\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta_0\text{ and }u\in[0,1].$$
The variable $p(X)$ is the observed p-value when the data are $X$. The
validity condition is distributional; measurability alone does not imply it.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let $A\in\mathcal F$.
Then the indicator $\mathbf 1_A$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A]=\mathbb P(A).$$

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

derivations.claim: Fix $u\in[0,1]$ and $H\in\mathcal F_1$. The event $\{p_N\le u\}$ is measurable by the p-value statistic definition [F2]. The events $D_m$, $m\in M$, are pairwise disjoint and partition $\Omega$. Countable additivity [F3] gives $P_0(H\cap\{p_N\le u\})=\sum_{m\in M}P_0(H\cap D_m\cap\{p_N\le u\})$ and $P_0(H)=\sum_{m\in M}P_0(H\cap D_m)$. Summing the assumed stratum inequalities over the increasing enumeration of $M$ (equivalently, taking finite partial sums and then their limits) yields $P_0(H\cap\{p_N\le u\})\le uP_0(H)$.

Let $Y_u$ be a version of $E_0[\mathbf1_{\{p_N\le u\}}\mid\mathcal F_1]$, which exists by [A1] and [F1]. The event identities in [F1] and [F4] turn step 1.1 into $\int_HY_u\,dP_0\le uP_0(H)$ for every $H\in\mathcal F_1$. Also $Y_u\ge0$ almost surely by [F5]. If $P_0(Y_u>u)>0$, then for some integer $k\ge1$ the set $H_k=\{Y_u\ge u+1/k\}\in\mathcal F_1$ has positive probability, because $\{Y_u>u\}=\bigcup_{k\ge1}H_k$. Monotonicity [F6] gives $\int_{H_k}Y_u\,dP_0\ge(u+1/k)P_0(H_k)>uP_0(H_k)$, contradicting the preceding event-integral bound. Thus $Y_u\le u$ almost surely. The argument is for each fixed $u$ and does not assert a common exceptional set over uncountably many thresholds.

boundaries.evidence: M is stipulated nonempty in the positive integers; step 1.1 partitions by every member.
At u=0 the stratum inequalities in step 1.1 force zero conditional rejection probability in step 2.1.
At u=1 the probability is bounded by one; steps 1.1 and 2.1 include this endpoint.
If M has one element, the finite partition in step 1.1 has one stratum and step 2.1 proves its conditional bound.
Both u=0 and u=1 are included in steps 1.1 and 2.1.
M is a given subset of the positive integers and is summed in its canonical increasing order in step 1.1; AC is used only for the conditional-expectation class in step 2.1.

boundaries.reason: The Statement is one implication, not an iff.
The Statement is one implication, not an iff.

risk_review.notes: Read both proof steps, all eight actual dependency carriers and reader/refuter evidence. For each fixed u, the countable partition by measurable D_m gives the event inequality for every interim H; a positive-probability superlevel H_k contradicts it and yields the conditional bound. Empty strata and finite/singleton M cause no problem; u=0 and u=1 are included. Nonnegative-integral monotonicity is applied on H_k, where Y_u is positive; no infinite scalar product arises. AC is inherited solely for CE existence. No joint uncountable exceptional-set assertion is made. J-STAGE printed S34-S35 and S40 map to PDF pages 2-3 and 8; Minas section 5.4.1 supports conditional calibration. Reader source-locator edits retained.

Since $0\le\mathbf1_{R_j}\le1$ for $j=0,1$, order preservation and the constant rule in [F2] give $0\le A,Q\le1$ almost surely. derivations.claim: Conditional order and the constant rule [F5] give $0\le A\le1$ almost surely. Clipping a version on the measurable null set where it leaves $[0,1]$ preserves its conditional-expectation class and changes $R_2$ only on a null set, so take $0\le A\le1$ everywhere. For each integer $n\ge1$, define $A_n=2^{-n}\lceil2^nA\rceil$. Its level sets are $\{A_n=0\}=\{A=0\}$ and $\{A_n=k2^{-n}\}=\{(k-1)2^{-n}<A\le k2^{-n}\}$ for $1\le k\le2^n$, so they are in $\mathcal F_1$. The inequality $\lceil2x\rceil\le2\lceil x\rceil$ shows $A_{n+1}\le A_n$, and $0\le A_n-A<2^{-n}$, hence $A_n$ is finite-valued and $A_n\downarrow A$. Write its values as $t_{n,k}=k2^{-n}$, $k=0,\ldots,2^n$, and put $S_{n,k}=\{A_n=t_{n,k}\}$. By [F2], the events $\{p_2\le t_{n,k}\}$ are measurable. Let $Q_n=E_0[\mathbf1_{\{p_2\le A_n\}}\mid\mathcal F_1]$. The disjoint partition by $S_{n,k}$, linearity [F5], and taking out the bounded known indicator [F3] give $Q_n=\sum_{k=0}^{2^n}\mathbf1_{S_{n,k}}E_0[\mathbf1_{\{p_2\le t_{n,k}\}}\mid\mathcal F_1]\le\sum_{k=0}^{2^n}t_{n,k}\mathbf1_{S_{n,k}}=A_n$ almost surely. For all $n$ these inequalities hold on one probability-one set, because only countably many fixed dyadic thresholds occur.

The events $B_n=\{p_2\le A_n\}$ decrease to $B=\{p_2\le A\}$. Their complement indicators are bounded and hence integrable, and increase to $\mathbf1_{B^c}$. Thus [F4] gives $E_0[\mathbf1_{B_n^c}\mid\mathcal F_1]\uparrow E_0[\mathbf1_{B^c}\mid\mathcal F_1]$ almost surely. By linearity and the constant rule [F5], this is equivalent to $Q_n\downarrow Q:=E_0[\mathbf1_B\mid\mathcal F_1]$. Taking limits in step 1.1 and using $A_n\downarrow A$ yields $Q\le A$ almost surely.

Apply [F6] to $R_2=B$: its conditional rejection probability is the $Q$ of step 2.1 and is at most $A$, while the original conditional-error budget has expectation at most $\alpha$. Therefore $P_0(R_2)\le\alpha$.

derivations.claim: Put $\Omega=\{0,1\}^4$ with the uniform law and let $I,B_0,B_2,B_3$ be the independent fair-bit coordinates. Define $p_j=1/2$ when $B_j=0$ and $p_j=1$ when $B_j=1$, for $j\in\{0,2,3\}$. Each $p_j$ is measurable with values in $[0,1]$, and its null CDF is $0$ for $u<1/2$, $1/2$ for $1/2\le u<1$, and $1$ at $u=1$, so each is a valid p-value by [F3]. Let $\mathcal F_1=\sigma(I)$, select $N=2$ on $I=0$ and $N=3$ on $I=1$, and take the original rejection event $R_0=\{p_0\le1/2\}$. Independence and [A1, F4] give its conditional error $A=E_0[\mathbf1_{R_0}\mid\mathcal F_1]=1/2$ almost surely; [F5] makes the resulting event probabilities version-independent. For each $m\in\{2,3\}$ and $H\in\mathcal F_1$, independence of $B_m$ from $I$ gives $P_0(H\cap\{N=m\}\cap\{p_N\le u\})=c(u)P_0(H\cap\{N=m\})$, where $c(u)=0$ for $u<1/2$, $1/2$ for $1/2\le u<1$, and $1$ for $u=1$; in every case $c(u)\le u$. Thus [F1] makes $p_N$ conditionally superuniform. Rejection at $A=1/2$ is exactly the event that the selected bit is zero. Since $P_0(R_0)=P_0(B_0=0)=1/2$, set $\alpha=1/2$ in the overall conclusion of [F2] to obtain $P_0(p_N\le A)\le1/2$; the selected bit is fair, so equality holds and the original budget is attained.

The positive density makes $\Phi$ continuous and strictly increasing. Define the one-sided stage p-values $p_i=1-\Phi(Z_i)$, so $Z_i=\Phi^{-1}(1-p_i)$; for $0<u<1$, $P_0(p_i\le u)=P_0(Z_i\ge\Phi^{-1}(1-u))=u$, and the endpoint inequalities are immediate, so they are valid by [F3]. Fix $c>0$ and set $\alpha=\int_c^\infty\phi(t)\,dt$, with $0<\alpha<1/2$ by positivity and evenness. Under the fixed equal-weight inverse-normal rule, reject when $W=(Z_1+Z_2)/\sqrt2\ge c$. The orthogonal change of variables $w=(z_1+z_2)/\sqrt2$, $v=(z_1-z_2)/\sqrt2$ has absolute Jacobian $1$ and satisfies $z_1^2+z_2^2=w^2+v^2$, so the joint density transforms to $\phi(w)\phi(v)$ and integration over $w\ge c$ gives the fixed-rule null rejection probability $\alpha$.

Choose $N_2=1$ when $Z_1\ge0$ and $N_2=2$ when $Z_1<0$. Without recalibrating $c$, use weights $w(N_2)=(1,0)$ in the first case and $(0,1)$ in the second; each has squared norm one. Since $c>0$, the adapted rejection event is the disjoint union $\{Z_1\ge c\}\cup\{Z_1<0,Z_2\ge c\}$, whose probability by independence is $\alpha+(1/2)\alpha=3\alpha/2>\alpha$. Thus unit-norm weights selected with the stage-2 size do not by themselves preserve the fixed-rule error probability.
